The Qatar Jet, a Mayor's Arrest, and a Week of Executive Testing

Foreign gifts, detained dissidents, and a Supreme Court pushback on deportation power defined a turbulent week

```markdown This was a week in which the machinery of American government strained visibly against its own limits, and in which the courts, more than any other institution, kept pulling that machinery back toward its constitutional moorings. Over seven days, a president moved to accept a $400 million jet from a foreign monarchy, a sitting mayor was arrested at a protest, a deputy chief of staff floated suspending one of the oldest legal protections against arbitrary detention, and the Supreme Court twice intervened to stop the executive branch from moving faster than the law allowed. By week's end, the president himself was publicly uncertain whether due process was a right at all.

The weekend set the tone. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, suggested the administration was weighing whether to suspend habeas corpus — the centuries-old legal mechanism that prevents the government from holding people without charge or judicial review. Republican senators, asked about the remark, declined to say it was off the table. The same weekend brought confirmation that the administration intended to accept a Boeing 747-8 valued at roughly $400 million from Qatar's royal family, intended for use as Air Force One, with White House counsel and the Department of Justice concluding it broke no bribery or emoluments law. In Newark, ICE agents arrested Mayor Ras Baraka while he stood outside a private detention facility alongside members of Congress; the Department of Homeland Security suggested the lawmakers present might face arrest as well. Elsewhere, the Pentagon ordered military academies to disregard race and sex in admissions and directed the removal of DEI and gender-related books from base libraries, extending political directives into military education. Federal courts, meanwhile, were already pushing back on immigration enforcement — blocking a deportation to Libya, ordering the release of Turkish student Rümeysa Öztürk, and halting removals of Venezuelan detainees to conditions resembling El Salvador's mega-prison. A coalition of Democratic state attorneys general sued over the dismantling of the Department of Health and Human Services, after roughly 10,000 employees were fired and entire agencies shuttered.

By Monday, the Qatar jet had become the week's most persistent thread. Reports detailed the administration's legal rationale even as scrutiny of the emoluments clause intensified. Trump signed an executive order aiming to tie U.S. drug prices to the lowest prices paid abroad, a move critics — including Senator Bernie Sanders — predicted would collapse in court for lack of legislative authority. SpaceX secured a $6 billion Pentagon contract and remained a frontrunner for the proposed "Golden Dome" missile shield, prompting more than 40 members of Congress to demand review of Elon Musk's influence after a nominated Inspector General was fired. The United States and China reached a Geneva agreement sharply reducing tariffs — from 145 percent to 30 percent — continuing a pattern of abrupt reversals in trade policy. The head of the U.S. Copyright Office was dismissed shortly after publishing a report skeptical of rushing government intervention on AI and copyright, a firing that read, to many observers, as retaliation for an inconvenient finding. Beneath these headline events, courts processed a steady stream of filings across immigration, agency-cuts, and tariff litigation — evidence that judicial review was operating continuously, even when it wasn't making headlines.

Tuesday sharpened the Qatar story into a direct confrontation between the legislative and executive branches. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer announced he would block all Justice Department nominations until the White House answered questions about the jet's constitutionality, demanding that Attorney General Pam Bondi testify. Republicans, for their part, still would not disavow Miller's habeas corpus comments, even as Trump's own remarks about upholding the Constitution remained notably vague. In Pennsylvania, a federal judge allowed conditional use of the Alien Enemies Act to speed deportation of accused Venezuelan gang members — but only with three weeks' notice and an opportunity to contest removal, a ruling that set up further Supreme Court review. The Qatar entanglements multiplied further: the Trump Organization struck a $5.5 billion golf resort deal in the country, and the U.S. approved a $2 billion arms sale to the same government whose jet gift was under scrutiny. Trump also signed an executive order aimed at dismantling the Department of Education, an action critics said bypassed Congress's authority over federal agencies entirely.

Wednesday was the week's densest day, its developments pulling in several directions at once. Attorney General Bondi — who had previously worked as a registered representative for the Qatari government — concluded that transferring the jet to the Defense Department and eventually to Trump's presidential library was legally permissible, a ruling whose independence was immediately questioned given her prior client. Hours later, the U.S. and Qatar signed a $243 billion defense and aviation agreement, including Qatar's purchase of up to 210 Boeing aircraft and more than $38 billion in future defense investment — a deal signed the same week as the disputed jet, deepening the sense that personal and state interests were becoming difficult to separate. On the immigration front, federal judges ordered the release of three detained activists — Badar Khan Suri, Rümeysa Öztürk, and Mohsen Mahdawi — rejecting the government's argument that their pro-Palestinian speech justified detention on foreign policy grounds. The Justice Department, meanwhile, announced plans to investigate former prosecutors who had brought cases against Trump, including Jack Smith, Alvin Bragg, and Fani Willis — a move distinct from the mayor's arrest days earlier, but part of the same broader pattern of law enforcement being turned toward political opponents. The Supreme Court heard oral arguments on Trump's executive order seeking to deny birthright citizenship to children born in the U.S. to noncitizen parents; even justices generally sympathetic to the administration asked skeptical questions — a separate legal matter from the Alien Enemies Act cases running in parallel. In the House, Republicans advanced budget proposals cutting Medicaid, SNAP, and child tax credit eligibility for mixed-status families, and Capitol Police arrested 25 disability rights protesters during the debate. A provision advanced alongside it would let the Treasury Secretary strip nonprofits of tax-exempt status on loosely defined "terrorist supporting" grounds. Away from Washington, the owner of the Los Angeles Times intervened to block a Kamala Harris endorsement and spike a mildly critical op-ed on Trump's cabinet picks, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was found to have quietly rerouted his own wife's flight away from Newark Airport even as he publicly insisted the airport, beset by radar outages and controller shortages, was safe.

Thursday brought the week's clearest resolution to an escalating legal question. The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that the administration must halt deportations of alleged gang members under the Alien Enemies Act without adequate due process, rejecting a 12-hour notice period the government had proposed as insufficient under the Fifth Amendment — the culmination of a thread that had run from Tuesday's conditional lower-court ruling to this definitive check. The House Budget Committee, meanwhile, voted down the broader reconciliation bill 16–21, as Freedom Caucus members demanded deeper cuts, exposing Republican divisions that stalled Trump's tax and spending agenda. Moody's downgraded the United States' credit rating for the first time since 1917, citing federal deficits projected to reach nearly 9 percent of GDP by 2035 — a distinct economic signal, separate from the week's tariff and trade news, about confidence in federal fiscal management. The administration terminated nearly 600 Voice of America contractors, most of them journalists, in defiance of a standing court order to maintain operations; many now face deportation because their visas were tied to their jobs. Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard fired the acting chair and deputy chair of the National Intelligence Council after their analysis contradicted Trump's claims about Venezuela's ties to a Salvadoran gang. Amid this, Newark's airport crisis worsened, operating with just three of fourteen required air traffic controllers, a shortfall linked to earlier federal cuts. Ben & Jerry's co-founder Ben Cohen was arrested protesting during a Senate hearing, and in Omaha, voters elected Democrat John Ewing as the city's first Black mayor, unseating a Republican incumbent in what was widely read as a rebuke of Trump-aligned politics — a reminder that ordinary electoral processes continued even amid the turbulence.

The week closed on a note of stark contrast. On Friday, Trump publicly questioned whether people in the United States have a right to due process at all, despite its explicit guarantee under the Fifth Amendment — remarks that landed just a day after the Supreme Court had enforced exactly that right. The Court formalized its injunction in A.A.R.P. v. Trump, blocking Alien Enemies Act deportations pending further proceedings, with Justices Alito and Thomas dissenting, and remanded the case to the Fifth Circuit — bringing the week's central legal arc to a firm, if temporary, resolution. A federal judge in South Dakota separately blocked the deportation of Priya Saxena, an Indian doctoral graduate whose student visa had been revoked over a minor traffic violation, extending the week's pattern of judicial pushback against aggressive visa actions. Inside the Democratic Party, a subcommittee recommended invalidating the vice-chair election of David Hogg and Malcolm Kenyatta over procedural irregularities — a minor but telling sign of internal strain. And in two unrelated but resonant notes, Harvard Law School confirmed that a document long believed to be a copy was in fact an original 1300 Magna Carta, one of only seven surviving originals, while Bruce Springsteen, performing in Manchester, criticized the abandonment of allies and deportations carried out without due process.

Taken together, the week offered a case study in how constitutional systems are tested — not through a single dramatic rupture, but through accumulation: a foreign gift accepted and then legally blessed by an official with ties to the giver; a mayor arrested for standing outside a detention facility; a due process guarantee affirmed by the Supreme Court and then publicly questioned by the president himself days later; prosecutors threatened with investigation for prior cases; journalists and intelligence analysts dismissed for producing unwelcome findings. Against all of this, courts functioned as the most consistent counterweight, intervening repeatedly and, in the case of the Alien Enemies Act, decisively. Whether that check holds, or whether rhetoric about suspending habeas corpus and doubting due process hardens into policy, will depend on what comes next — but this week made clear how many fronts were open at once, and how much weight the judiciary was being asked to bear. ```
